claims.claim: The poc1 mutant in Tetrahymena causes partial loss of the A-C linker and defects in triplet microtubule organization.
claims.source: No components of the A-C linker have been identified, but the poc1 mutant in Tetrahymena causes partial loss of this linker and defects in triplet microtubule organization (Meehl et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin likely work together in a critical aspect of centriole structure and function.
claims.source: Here we have shown that delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin likely work together in a critical aspect of centriole structure and function, and that cells lacking either tubulin undergo a futile cycle of de novo centriole formation and disintegration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: In human cells, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin act to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next.
claims.source: Our results show that in human cells, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin act to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next, perhaps by stabilizing the main structural feature of centrioles, the triplet microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin may stabilize centriole structures by stabilizing the triplet microtubules.
claims.source: Our results show that in human cells, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin act to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next, perhaps by stabilizing the main structural feature of centrioles, the triplet microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

results.result: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− human cells lack triplet microtubules and instead contain only singlet microtubules, as demonstrated by electron microscopy showing reduced outer diameter (172.5 nm ±13 nm for TUBD1−/− and 174.6 nm ±8 nm for TUBE1−/−) compared to control mother centrioles (222.9 ± 9 nm).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C43-C50 provide converging evidence from correlative light-electron microscopy (CLEM) and quantitative measurements. The EM cross-sections directly visualize singlet microtubules (C45), and the diameter measurements (C46-C49) are statistically significant and consistent with singlet rather than triplet structure. The sample sizes are adequate (n=17 for TUBD1−/−, n=13 for TUBE1−/−, n=24 for control mother centrioles) and the measurements align with prior literature on centriole dimensions.

results.result: Mutant centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells have a slightly reduced central lumen diameter compared to controls, which is consistent with observations in normal procentrioles with singlet microtubules prior to triplet elaboration.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by quantitative EM measurements shown in Figure 1E and comparison to prior literature (Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982). The observation is internally consistent with the singlet microtubule phenotype and provides additional structural characterization.

results.result: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells undergo normal cell cycle-dependent elongation despite lacking triplet microtubules, as measured by both electron microscopy length measurements and CP110-SASS6 separation distances that increase from ~0.3 μm in interphase to ~0.5 μm in mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C62 provide complementary evidence from EM (direct length measurements) and immunofluorescence (CP110-SASS6 separation). The interphase lengths of mutant centrioles (222 nm for TUBD1−/−, 339 nm for TUBE1−/−) are similar to control procentrioles (207 nm), and both show ~200 nm elongation by G2-M. The mitotic TUBE1−/− centrioles show a distinctive two-segment morphology (C57) with combined length approximating mature centrioles. Sample sizes are adequate and measurements are quantitative.

results.result: POC5, a marker of the distal compartment, is absent from centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, suggesting that doublet microtubules of the extended centriole distal end are required for defining this compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2E showing POC5 presence in control mitotic centrioles and absence in mutant centrioles. The inference (C66) is reasonable given that mutant centrioles lack doublet microtubules and fail to recruit POC5. However, the mechanism is not directly tested.

results.result: TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells show an aberrant centriole distribution with ~50% of cells having five or more centriole foci and ~50% having no detectable centrioles, in contrast to the normal distribution in control cells. This phenotype is rescued by expression of the respective tubulins, and mutant centrioles are never closely apposed as in wild-type cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C73 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A,B showing centriole number distributions across multiple independent cell lines. The rescue experiments (C72, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) provide strong evidence that the phenotype is specifically due to loss of delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin. The observation that centrioles are never closely apposed (C73) is consistent with de novo formation rather than duplication.

results.result: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells lack maturation markers: all lack Cep164 (distal appendage marker), most lack detectable gamma-tubulin (pericentriolar material), and most retain SASS6 (cartwheel protein normally lost at mitosis-interphase transition).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C showing absence of Cep164 and reduced gamma-tubulin in mutant centrioles, while SASS6 persists. The quantification shows ~40% of control centrioles are Cep164-positive (consistent with the maturation cycle) while mutant centrioles are all negative. This supports the interpretation that mutant centrioles fail to mature and persist through the cell cycle.

results.result: Aberrant centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells are formed in S-phase, persist into mitosis, and are absent in G1, with loss occurring at a specific event at the mitosis-interphase transition rather than simply time-dependent degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by cell cycle-staged immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D. The observation that centrioles persist during 24-hour G2 arrest but are lost after mitosis (C81) provides strong evidence for a specific mitosis-dependent disintegration event rather than time-dependent decay. The experimental design appropriately controls for time effects.

results.result: Time-course experiments after mitotic shakeoff show that TUBE1−/− cells have centrioles in mitosis, lose them progressively in the first 3 hours of G1 (50% by 1 hour), and reform them de novo when cells enter S-phase at 12 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by quantitative time-course data in Figure 3E. The temporal pattern clearly shows centriole loss in early G1 and reformation in S-phase, with appropriate cell cycle markers (PCNA for S-phase entry). The data provide strong evidence for the futile cycle of formation and disintegration.

results.result: Live cell imaging shows that centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells do not persist into the next interphase, and the mitotic interval is prolonged (106 min ±43 min, n=10) compared to control cells (46 min ±6 min, n=11), similar to acentriolar human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by live cell imaging data in Figure 3F and Videos 1-2. The quantitative measurements of mitotic interval are provided with appropriate sample sizes and error estimates. The comparison to prior literature on acentriolar cells (C90) provides context. However, the large standard deviation in TUBE1−/− mitotic interval (±43 min) suggests substantial cell-to-cell variability.

results.result: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin are not required to initiate centriole formation in human cells, as evidenced by the fact that aberrant centrioles form in mutant cells and that de novo centrioles formed after centrinone washout persist normally through mitosis and G1.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by the observation that mutant cells form centriole structures (albeit unstable ones) and by the centrinone washout control experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) showing that de novo centrioles can be stable. This distinguishes the mutant phenotype from a general defect in de novo centriole formation and supports the conclusion that the tubulins are specifically required for stability rather than initiation.

results.result: Paclitaxel treatment stabilizes aberrant centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells such that they persist into G1, without preventing elongation or restoring gamma-tubulin recruitment or SASS6 cartwheel retention, suggesting that preventing microtubule depolymerization is sufficient for structural stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are supported by drug treatment experiments in Figure 4A-D. The paclitaxel rescue is specific (centrioles persist with paclitaxel but not DMSO control) and the measurements show that elongation still occurs (C93) while maturation markers remain absent (C96-C97). The quantification of SASS6 loss (97% ± 2% cells lack SASS6 foci) is rigorous. The proposed mechanism (C98) is reasonable but remains inferential.

results.result: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin physically interact as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation, suggesting they may dimerize to form higher-order structures similar to alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 and C12 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E showing specific interaction between epsilon-tubulin and delta-tubulin but not with GFP control. The speculation about dimerization (C101) is reasonable by analogy to alpha/beta-tubulin but is not directly tested. The interaction data support the similar phenotypes of the two mutants and suggest functional cooperation.

results.result: Evolutionary analysis shows that triplet microtubule presence is not strictly correlated with delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin presence (e.g., Drosophila and Ginkgo biloba have triplets but lack these tubulins), suggesting that these tubulins are required for stabilization rather than formation of triplet microtubules in most organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 are supported by evolutionary analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The phylogenetic argument is logically sound: independent loss of these tubulins in dipteran insects and plants, both of which retain triplet microtubules, suggests triplet formation per se does not require these tubulins. The inference that they function in stabilization (C107) is consistent with the experimental data showing unstable singlet microtubules in mutants. However, this remains an inference based on evolutionary parsimony rather than direct experimental evidence.

results.result: Organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin have simpler centriole structures that lack typical distal appendages and often lack a distal compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are supported by comparative analysis of centriole structures across organisms. This observation provides evolutionary context for the experimental findings showing loss of distal compartment markers (POC5) and maturation markers (Cep164) in mutant cells.

results.result: Homozygous null mutations of TUBD1 or TUBE1 could only be isolated in TP53−/− cells, and multiple independent cell lines were generated with compound heterozygous mutations predicted to be null or strong loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 are supported by sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The requirement for TP53−/− background is consistent with prior literature showing p53-dependent arrest upon centriole loss (C35). The molecular characterization of the mutations (frameshifts, premature stops, deletion of start codon) supports the conclusion that these are likely null alleles. Multiple independent lines with similar phenotypes strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Aberrant centrioles with elongated singlet microtubules become unstable as cells progress through mitosis, and disintegration can be suppressed by paclitaxel treatment. The authors note that ciliary axonemes with doublet microtubules can be dynamic but disassembly is slow and regulated, and that non-tubulin densities have been identified in cryoEM structures.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is a summary of experimental findings that are well-supported. Claims C111-C113 provide context from prior literature about microtubule dynamics in other structures. These contextual claims are appropriately cited and help frame the discussion of possible mechanisms.

results.result: POC5 is not recruited to singlet microtubule centrioles, and the authors speculate that POC5 may bind to and stabilize doublet microtubules in the distal compartment.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 is directly supported by immunofluorescence data. Claim C115 is explicitly labeled as speculation and represents a reasonable hypothesis based on the data, but is not experimentally tested. The speculation is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin work together in a critical aspect of centriole structure and function, acting to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance from one cell cycle to the next, perhaps by stabilizing triplet microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing the experimental findings. The conclusion that the tubulins work together (C117) is supported by similar phenotypes and physical interaction. The conclusion about stabilization for inheritance (C118) is well-supported by the cell cycle analysis and paclitaxel rescue. The proposed mechanism involving triplet stabilization (C119) is reasonable but remains somewhat speculative, appropriately qualified with 'perhaps.'

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on centriole structure, the centriole duplication cycle, tubulin family members, and prior work on delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin in unicellular eukaryotes and mammals.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout the manuscript. They provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings but are not novel results of this study.

results.result: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells fail to undergo centriole maturation, and triplet microtubules are necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 about failure of maturation are supported by the absence of maturation markers (Cep164, gamma-tubulin, POC5) documented in multiple experiments. Claim C13 about triplet microtubules being necessary for inheritance is a key conclusion inferred from the observation that centrioles lacking triplets do not persist to the next cell cycle. This inference is well-supported by the totality of the data, though it remains an inference rather than a direct demonstration of causality.

results.result: Aberrant centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells are formed de novo each cell cycle but are unstable and do not persist to the next cell cycle, leading to a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 represent a central conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence: cell cycle-staged analysis (C78-C81), time-course experiments (C82-C85), live imaging (C86-C90), and marker analysis (C74-C77). The characterization as a 'futile cycle' (C10) is an appropriate interpretation of the repeated formation and loss pattern.

results.result: Many TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells in an asynchronous population had multiple, unpaired centrin foci that also labeled with centriolar proteins CP110 and SASS6.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 1A and 3A showing multiple centrin foci that colocalize with CP110 and SASS6. This establishes that the observed structures are centriole-related and provides the basis for subsequent CLEM analysis.
